ancient.name: Sima de los Huesos
ancient.story_individual:
Around 400,000 years ago, a hominin died and their remains ended up in what would become known as Sima de los Huesos (Pit of Bones) in northern Spain. The individual's remains, including a femur which would later yield crucial DNA evidence, were preserved alongside approximately 28 other individuals in the cave system at Atapuerca. While researchers cannot determine this individual's biological sex, they know they belonged to a population that showed Neanderthal-like features in their skeletal morphology.

The remarkable preservation of their DNA was made possible by the stable, cold conditions within the cave. When the femur was analyzed in 2014, the DNA retrieved from it represented the oldest human DNA ever sequenced, pushing back the boundaries of ancient DNA research by hundreds of thousands of years. The mitochondrial DNA unexpectedly showed closer affinity to Denisovans than to Neanderthals, despite the skeletal characteristics of the population.

The recovery of such ancient DNA was a major technical achievement that required innovative methods to deal with highly degraded genetic material. While we don't know the details of this individual's life - what they ate, how they lived, or how they died - their genetic legacy has provided crucial insights into human evolution and the complex relationships between ancient hominin populations.

Subsequent nuclear DNA analysis of Sima de los Huesos hominins revealed a closer connection to Neanderthals than the mtDNA initially suggested, adding another fascinating layer to this individual's story.

References

  • Meyer, M., Fu, Q., Aximu-Petri, A. et al. A mitochondrial genome sequence of a hominin from Sima de los Huesos. Nature 505, 403–406 (2014). https://doi.org/10.1038/nature12788

  • Meyer, M., Arsuaga, JL., de Filippo, C. et al. Nuclear DNA sequences from the Middle Pleistocene Sima de los Huesos hominins. Nature 531, 504–507 (2016). https://doi.org/10.1038/nature17405

Pictured: Cranium 17 of the Sima de los Huesos, from an individual from the same location and time period. Nohemi Sala, Juan Luis Arsuaga, Ana Pantoja-Pérez, Adrián Pablos, Ignacio Martínez, Rolf M. Quam, Asier Gómez-Olivencia, José María Bermúdez de Castro, Eudald Carbonell, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

famous.name: Saint Henry
famous.story_individual:
Saint Henry, also known as Henry II (Heinrich II), was Holy Roman Emperor from 1014 and King of East Francia from 1002, the last ruler of the Ottonian dynasty. He was the son of Henry II, Duke of Bavaria, and Gisela of Burgundy, and belonged to the Bavarian branch of the Liudolfing, or Ottonian, house. Through his father, he descended from the line of emperors established by Otto the Great, while through his mother he was tied to the Burgundian royal family. By birth and inheritance alike, Henry stood within one of the most important ruling dynasties of early medieval Europe.

Henry came to power in 1002 after a contested succession and spent much of his reign restoring royal authority, managing the great nobles of the empire, and reinforcing the partnership between kingship and the Church. More than most medieval rulers, he became associated with ecclesiastical patronage, royal support for bishops, and the use of church institutions as pillars of imperial government. In 1014, he was crowned Holy Roman Emperor in Rome by Pope Benedict VIII, confirming his position at the head of the empire. Later canonized as a saint, Henry acquired a legacy that was not only political and dynastic, but also explicitly religious.

His dynastic significance was shaped in part by the fact that he was the last of his line to hold the imperial office. His marriage to Cunigunde of Luxembourg linked him to another major noble family of the empire, but the couple left no children. With Henry’s death in 1024, Ottonian rule came to an end. His reign therefore marks the final phase of a dynasty that had remained central to imperial politics for generations.

Genetic analysis is adding another dimension to our understanding of Henry’s life and identity. Analysis of Henry’s remains from Bamberg Cathedral has shown that he belonged to Y-DNA haplogroup R-FTA63331, a paternal lineage so far observed only rarely in present-day testers, including single representatives from Germany, the Netherlands, Denmark, and South Africa. His maternal haplogroup is H7b2a1'3, a lineage identified in testers across western Europe and the Alpine region. Genetic sequencing was carried out by the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology, while Y-chromosomal and mitochondrial DNA analysis was performed by FamilyTreeDNA. The identification of Henry’s remains was also supported by comparison with his great-uncle Otto the Great, whose sequenced remains showed the expected autosomal relationship and carried the same Y-DNA lineage.

Reference

  • Ringbauer, H., Wozniak, T., Feuchter, J., Runfeldt, G., Bianco, R. A., Zhang, G., Prüfer, K., Orschiedt, J., Simm, A., Maier, P., Sager, M., Dresely, V., Krause, J., Meller, H., & Wehner, D. (2026). Reconstructing their genomes confirms the historically attested genealogy of the two medieval emperors Otto I (“the Great”) and Heinrich II (“Saint Henry”). bioRxiv. https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.03.18.712637

Pictured: Depiction of Holy Roman Emperor Henry II, 15th century. Moravian Gallery in Brno, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

famous.name: Anna of Antioch
famous.story_individual:
Agnes of Antioch was Queen of Hungary from 1172 to 1184. Born to Raynald of Châtillon and Constance, Princess of Antioch, she came from a prestigious lineage of powerful women in the Crusader States. Through her maternal line, she was the granddaughter of Alice of Jerusalem, princess of Antioch, and great-granddaughter of Morphia of Melitene, an Armenian noblewoman who served as queen consort of Jerusalem through her marriage to Baldwin II.

Around 1170, Agnes went to Constantinople where her older half-sister Maria was the wife of Byzantine Emperor Manuel I Comnenus. There she married Béla (then known as Caesar Alexios), and received the name Anna at the imperial court. The exact date of their marriage is debated by historians, with suggestions ranging from 1168 to 1172. Before coming to Hungary, the couple made a pilgrimage to Jerusalem where they donated to the Knights Hospitaller.

Following the death of King Stephen III in March 1172, Béla ascended to the Hungarian throne. Anna was crowned queen alongside him at the Cathedral Basilica of Saint Stephen in Székesfehérvár on January 13, 1173. As queen, she had a significant cultural impact on Hungary. She influenced the spread of French cultural patterns and was connected to the arrival of the first Cistercian monks from Burgundy. She also introduced the practice of public bathing to Hungary, drawing from her experiences in Constantinople and Antioch.

Anna and Béla had six children, including two future Hungarian kings: Emeric and Andrew II. Through her children, she became the ancestress of all subsequent Hungarian kings, as well as various royal lines across Central Europe.

She died around 1184 and was buried in the Cathedral Basilica of Székesfehérvár. Her remains, along with those of her husband Béla III and other medieval royals, were later studied through genetic analysis in research published by Nagy et al. (2020) in collaboration with FamilyTreeDNA, and subsequently by Varga et al. (2023), providing scientific confirmation of her identity and relationships. Her tomb, rediscovered during the Hungarian Revolution of 1848, now rests in the Matthias Church in Budapest.

famous.name: Anne of Bohemia, Duchess of Silesia
famous.story_individual:
Anne of Bohemia, a member of the Přemyslid dynasty, was the daughter of Ottokar I of Bohemia and Constance of Hungary. Through her marriage to Henry II the Pious in 1216, she became Duchess of Silesia and, from 1238 to 1241, High Duchess consort of Poland. As consort to one of the most prominent Piast rulers of the age, she connected two of medieval Central Europe’s leading ruling houses: the Bohemian Přemyslids and the Polish Piasts.

Widowed in 1241 after Henry II’s death at the Battle of Legnica, Anne played an important political role in the years that followed, acting as regent for her sons during a period of instability. She was also a significant religious patron, associated especially with the Franciscan nuns in Wrocław, and is remembered as the founder and benefactor of the monastery of St Clare there.

As the wife of Henry II the Pious and mother of numerous Piast princes and princesses, Anne occupied a central place in the history of 13th-century Poland. Her children included Bolesław II the Bald, Henry III the White, and Konrad I of Głogów, all prominent figures in the later history of the Silesian Piasts. 

Her mtDNA haplogroup is H7b1, and she shares two additional mutations with her grandmother, Anne of Antioch.

Reference

famous.name: Ditchling man
famous.story_individual:
Ditchling man lived around 2200 BCE during the European Bronze Age. His remains were found in a burial near Ditchling Road in Brighton, England. He was associated with the Bell Beaker Britain cultural group. The Beaker people arrived in Great Britain during this time. They were likely farmers and had a large impact on the modern-British gene pool.

Sculptor and archaeologist Oscar D. Nilsson reconstructed the face of the man, and the model is on display at the Brighton Museum in England.

Olalde et al. 2018 studied the DNA of the man and many others in the large study “The Beaker phenomenon and the genomic transformation of northwest Europe.” The supplementary material describes the burial:

The Ditchling Road Beaker burial was excavated in 1921 as part of preparations for the eponymous road to the south of Stanmer Park in Brighton, Sussex. It consisted of a flat shallow earthen grave containing the skeleton of a 25-35-year-old male in a flexed position on his left side with his head to the northeast facing southeast. The skeleton was accompanied by barbed flint arrowhead recovered from beneath the skull and a Beaker positioned next to his legs. A quantity of snail shells from a variety of species had been placed in front of its mouth. The skeleton is curated at Brighton Museum and Art Gallery. Ancient DNA data from a sample of the petrous portion of the temporal bone of this individual were included in this study.

His direct maternal line belonged to mtDNA haplogroup H4a1a1a.

Reconstruction photo provided by O D Nilsson.

famous.name: Takabuti
famous.story_individual:
Takabuti was an ancient Egyptian noblewoman who lived in Thebes during the Twenty-fifth Dynasty, around 660 BCE. As the mistress of a great house, she held a position of significant social standing. Born to a prestigious family, her father Nespare served as a priest of Amun, and her mother was named Tasenirit.

Tragically, Takabuti's life was cut short between the ages of twenty and thirty. Recent scientific analysis revealed that she met a violent end, killed by an axe blow to her upper left shoulder that was likely instantly fatal. The circumstances of her death suggest she may have been trying to escape from an assailant, possibly during a period of conflict – perhaps at the hands of an Assyrian soldier or someone from her own community.

Takabuti possessed several unique physical characteristics. She had auburn hair, and two rare anatomical features: an extra tooth (found in only 0.02% of the population) and an extra vertebra (present in 2% of the population). Contrary to earlier beliefs about her mummification, her heart was not removed during the embalming process.

Takabuti Egyptian Mummy at Belfast Museum. Notafly, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Her mummified remains have had a fascinating afterlife. Following the Napoleonic Wars, during a period of active trade in Egyptian antiquities, Takabuti was purchased in 1834 by Thomas Greg of Ballymenoch House, Holywood, County Down. She made history as the first mummy to be unwrapped in Ireland, with this significant event taking place on January 27, 1835, at the Belfast Natural History Society's museum. The unwrapping generated considerable scientific interest, particularly in Belfast, then the commercial center of the Irish linen industry, which took special note of her fine linen wrappings.

Recent genetic analysis has revealed an unexpected aspect of Takabuti's ancestry. Her mitochondrial DNA belongs to haplogroup H4a1, a genetic lineage predominantly found in European populations. This rare genetic variant, found today in only about 2% of southern Iberians and 1% of Lebanese populations, suggests complex patterns of human movement between Europe and Egypt in ancient times. The presence of this European genetic marker in a high-status Egyptian woman from before the Greek and Roman periods challenges our understanding of ancient Egyptian society and its connections with other regions.

Today, nearly two centuries after her unwrapping, Takabuti continues to captivate visitors at the Ulster Museum in Belfast, Northern Ireland. Her well-preserved remains and the ongoing scientific discoveries about her life, death, and ancestry make her an invaluable window into the complex social and genetic landscape of ancient Egypt.

References

  • Drosou, K., Collin, T. C., Freeman, P. J., Loynes, R., & Freemont, T. (2020). The first reported case of the rare mitochondrial haplotype H4a1 in ancient Egypt. Scientific Reports, 10, 17037. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-020-74114-9

Biographical information sourced from Wikipedia. Biography in part generated using Anthropic (2025) Claude 3.5 Sonnet [Large language model].

famous.name: Slonk Hill man
famous.story_individual:
Slonk Hill man lived around 300 BCE during the Late Iron Age in Great Britain. He was about 24 years old when he died. His remains were found in a burial on Slonk Hill in Brighton, England. He was associated with the Iron Age Britain cultural group.

Sculptor and archaeologist Oscar D. Nilsson reconstructed the face of the man, and the model is on display at the Brighton Museum in England.

Patterson et al. 2021 studied the DNA of the man and many others in the large study “Large-scale migration into Britain during the Middle to Late Bronze Age”. The supplementary material describes the burial:

Rescue excavations on Slonk Hill, Brighton were undertaken by Brighton and Hove Archaeological Society in 1968–74 in advance of the building of a bridge over the River Adur. The excavations uncovered a small enclosed Iron Age settlement with occupation spanning the sixth–first centuries BCE and a later Romano-British settlement spanning the first/second–fourth centuries CE, incorporating two earlier Bronze Age barrows, as well as two Iron Age burials (Graves 1 and 2). Grave 1 comprised an oval-shaped storage pit containing the complete articulated skeleton of a male aged c. 24 years, flexed on his left side with his head to the north and his right hand in front of his face. The body had been placed on top of a layer of shells, mainly mussels, but also winkles and barnacles, which covered the bottom of the pit. The human remains were accompanied by a flint ‘Shepherd’s crown’ (a fossilised sea urchin) and some fragments of pottery dating typologically to the Iron Age. Further potsherds and the shaft of a small iron implement were recovered from the grave fill.

Grave 2 comprised a small purpose-built grave containing the skeleton of a female aged 35–45 years, buried flexed on her left side with her skull to the north, facing east. A shale bracelet was found on the left forearm and an involuted iron brooch was recovered from near her shoulder. The lower 23cm of grave fill included part of a quern stone and the right half of an ox sacrum.

…

aDNA analysis revealed that these two individuals are second or third degree relatives.

His direct maternal line belonged to mtDNA haplogroup H1.

Reconstruction photo provided by O D Nilsson.

famous.name: Sweyn II of Denmark
famous.story_individual:
Sweyn Estridsen was King of Denmark (Sweyn II) from 1047 to 1074. He took the matronymic surname Estridsson after his mother Estrid Svendsdatter, emphasizing his link to the Danish royal house through her lineage. Sweyn was the last Viking king of Denmark, and marked the transition between the Viking Age to the Middle Ages in Danish history.

He was married twice, first to Gyda of Sweden - daughter of King Anund Jacob - in 1047 and then to to Gunnhildr Sveinsdóttir in 1050. Sweyn fathered at least twenty children throughout his life, of whom only one was born in wedlock. Despite his complex personal life, he maintained strong ties with the church and was instrumental in strengthening Christianity in Denmark. His reign was notable for strengthening the Danish church, and establishing a stable succession of Danish kings through his many sons.

Reconstruction of Sweyn’s head from 1911 based on his cranium. Photo: Arne Kvitrud, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

His burial in Roskilde Cathedral began a tradition that would continue through the centuries, with the cathedral serving as the main burial church for Danish monarchs.

In a groundbreaking ancient DNA analysis published by Dissing et al. in 2007 titled "The last Viking King: A royal maternity case solved by ancient DNA analysis." His remains were genetically tested, and shown to belong to Haplogroup H. This finding became crucial in solving a historical mystery, as a separate DNA analysis of the tomb that was thought to contain his mother showed that she belonged to haplogroup H5a, making it impossible for her to have been his mother. The tomb is now believed to contain one of his daughters-in-law, possibly Margareta Hasbjörnsdatter, who was married to his son Harald Hen.

References

  • Dissing, J., Binladen, J., Hansen, A., Sejrsen, B., Willerslev, E., & Lynnerup, N. (2006). The last Viking King: A royal maternity case solved by ancient DNA analysis. Forensic Science International, 166(1), 21–27. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.forsciint.2006.03.020

Pictured: Coin of Sweyn Estridsen. Peter Christian Hauberg (1844-1928), Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons. Biography in part generated using Anthropic (2024) Claude 3 Opus [Large language model].

famous.name: Estrid of Denmark
famous.story_individual:
Estrid was a medieval Danish queen entombed in Roskilde Cathedral, Denmark's most sacred royal burial ground.

For centuries, the remains in this prestigious tomb were believed to be those of Estrid Svendsdatter, mother of King Sweyn II Estridsen, who ruled Denmark from 1047 to 1074. The fresco naming the tomb reads "Margrethe, alias Estrid, Queen of Denmark".

In 2007, the remains were studied and the results were published by Dissing et al. in their paper "The last Viking King: A royal maternity case solved by ancient DNA analysis".

A comparison of the mitochondrial DNA from Sweyn II’s remains and the remains believed to be Estrid's differed on two crucial positions. These differences assigned Sweyn to haplogroup H while the woman was in haplogroup H5a. This genetic evidence made it impossible for her to have been King Sven's mother.

While the entombed woman could not have been King Sweyn's mother, historical records indicate two daughter-in-laws of Sweyn also named Estrid who married into the Danish royal family and became queens.

Researchers suggest the remains may belong to one of these two women. One possibility is Margareta Hasbjörnsdatter (or Asbjørnsdatter) who was Queen consort of Denmark 1076–1080 as the spouse of Sweyn’s son Harald Hen (c. 1040–1080).

References

  • Dissing, J., Binladen, J., Hansen, A., Sejrsen, B., Willerslev, E., & Lynnerup, N. (2006). The last Viking King: A royal maternity case solved by ancient DNA analysis. Forensic Science International, 166(1), 21–27. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.forsciint.2006.03.020

famous.name: Birger Jarl
famous.story_individual:
Birger Jarl, also known as Birger Magnusson, was a Swedish statesman and regent from the House of Bjälbo who played a pivotal role in consolidating Sweden. He used the Latin title "dux sveorum et guttorum" (duke of Swedes and Geats).

Born around 1210, he spent his childhood in Bjälbo, Östergötland. His strategic marriage to Princess Ingeborg Eriksdotter, sister of King Erik XI, in the mid-1230s significantly strengthened his position. He became jarl (earl) in 1248 under King Erik and proved to be a powerful military leader, defeating the Folkung forces at the Battle of Sparrsätra in 1247 and establishing Swedish rule in Finland through the Second Swedish Crusade. When King Erik died in 1250, Birger's son Valdemar became king while Birger served as regent, holding the true power in Sweden.

After Ingeborg's death in 1254, he married Mechtilde of Holstein, widow of King Abel of Denmark, in 1261. Through his first marriage to Ingeborg, he had several children including King Valdemar and his successor King Magnus III. Birger is traditionally credited with the foundation of Stockholm around 1250, though historical records only show his interest in the location through two letters from 1252.

He died on October 21, 1266, at Jälbolung in Västergötland and was buried in Varnhem Abbey alongside his son Erik and his second wife Mechtilde. Their remains were rediscovered during restoration work in the 1920s and later confirmed through modern DNA analysis, which revealed Birger's mitochondrial haplogroup to be H.

References

  • Malmström, H., Vretemark, M., Tillmar, A., Durling, M. B., Skoglund, P., Gilbert, M. T. P., Willerslev, E., Holmlund, G., & Götherström, A. (2012). Finding the founder of Stockholm – A kinship study based on Y-chromosomal, autosomal and mitochondrial DNA. Annals of Anatomy - Anatomischer Anzeiger, 194(1), 138-145. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.aanat.2011.03.014

Pictured: Birger Jarl in Varnhem Church. Axel Forssén (1888-1961), Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons. Historical information sourced from Wikipedia. Biography in part generated using Anthropic (2025) Claude 3.5 Sonnet [Large language model].

famous.name: Agnes of Waiblingen
famous.story_individual:
Agnes of Waiblingen, also known as Agnes of Germany, Agnes of Franconia and Agnes of Saarbrücken, was a significant figure in medieval German history as the daughter of Holy Roman Emperor Henry IV and a key link between several powerful dynasties. Through her strategic marriages, she played a crucial role in shaping European politics.

First married at age 14 to Frederick I, Duke of Swabia, she had several children including Frederick II of Swabia and Conrad III, who would later become King of Germany. After Frederick's death in 1105, she married Leopold III, Margrave of Austria, with whom she had at least 11 children, including Otto of Freising, the famous medieval chronicler, and several other children who formed important political alliances through marriage.

When her brother Emperor Henry V died childless in 1125, Agnes inherited the extensive Salian family estates. This inheritance, combined with her marriages and numerous offspring, helped establish both the Hohenstaufen and Babenberg dynasties as powerful forces in medieval Germany.

An interesting fact about Agnes is that her second marriage inspired a famous legend: her lost veil, found years later by Leopold while hunting, allegedly led to his founding of the Klosterneuburg Monastery, which became an important religious and cultural center.

Her mtDNA haplogroup was reported in Christiane Maria Bauer et al, Molecular genetic investigations on Austria's patron saint Leopold III, Forensic Science International: Genetics, Volume 7, Issue 2, 2013. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.fsigen.2012.10.012

Biographical information sourced in part from Wikipedia and in part from Anthropic (2025) Claude 3.5 Sonnet [Large Language Model]. Pictured: 15th century painting of Agnes by Hans Part, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

famous.name: Neanderthal Man
famous.story_individual:
Neanderthals were first named and unearthed in 1856 in the Neander Valley of Germany, three full years before Darwin published his book On the Origin of Species. In his writings, Darwin only briefly wrote about human evolution and did not mention anything about the newly named Neanderthals. Coincidentally, by 1848, a Neanderthal skeleton had already been discovered in Gibraltar. That specimen, however, had remained uncharacterized in science. So, as fate would have it, the German team is credited with discovering the new species, and the name Neanderthal still remains. Neanderthal Man (seen pictured as a reconstruction) from Feldhofer cave in Neander Valley lived approximately 40,000 years ago.

Today, we know much more about these cousins of Homo sapiens (humans), when and where they lived and how they may have mated with our stone-age ancestors. In 2008, a team led by Nobel Laureate Svante Pääbo sequenced the first Neanderthal genome, and just months after that publication, anthropologists discovered that Neanderthal DNA still resided in most humans alive today. Yes, humans and Neanderthals had mated.

Although the common evolutionary ancestor to Homo sapiens and Neanderthals lived more than half-a-million years ago, we now know that the Y chromosome of the male Neanderthals sequenced to date came from an introduction event (a mating) between a male archaic human and a female Neanderthal between 370,000 and 100,000 years ago. This, and other new findings, suggests that mixing between human ancestors and Neanderthals occurred early and possibly frequently while they co-existed for millennia in Europe and Asia, which was until approximately 35,000 years ago when Neanderthals went extinct. 

We are fortunate to be living in an amazing time where every year new discoveries add exciting information about humans, our ancestors, and our shared prehistory. The last decade alone has completely reshaped our knowledge and relationship with the once mighty Neanderthals.

Homo neanderthalensis reconstruction - Mr. N

©Neanderthal Museum

The divergence time between modern human and Neanderthal Y chromosomes was estimated by Petr et al. 2020. The evolutionary history of Neanderthal and Denisovan Y chromosomes. The A000-T haplogroup name comes from the ISOGG Y-DNA Haplogroup Tree 2019-2020.
